title: Find the Way Back Before You Decide
summary: Many decisions feel permanent only because nobody has described how to undo them. How to tell one-way doors from two-way doors, and how to build the way back.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
The meeting has spent 40 minutes on one choice: turn on the new onboarding flow for everyone, or keep the old one? Everyone is talking as if the door will lock behind them. Then someone asks, "What would it take to undo this in two weeks?" The answer turns out to be one config change. The choice still matters, but it stops pretending to be permanent, and the meeting wraps up ten minutes later.

That question is one of the most useful a team can ask. This piece is about how to tell the decisions you can undo from the ones you can't, how to build the way back on purpose, and why it makes a team nicer to work in.

One-way doors and two-way doors

Jeff Bezos described this split in his 2015 letter to Amazon shareholders (2015 Letter to Shareholders). Some decisions are "consequential and irreversible or nearly irreversible". He called them one-way doors, or Type 1 decisions, and said they must be made "methodically, carefully, slowly". Most decisions aren't like that. They're "changeable, reversible", two-way doors, and he argued that these Type 2 decisions "can and should be made quickly by high judgment individuals or small groups."

The trap he named is the interesting part. As organizations grow, they tend to use the heavy Type 1 process on most decisions, two-way doors included. The result, in his words: "slowness, unthoughtful risk aversion, failure to experiment sufficiently, and consequently diminished invention." Teams a thousand times smaller than Amazon walk into the same trap every week.

Usually a two-way door Usually a one-way door
Copy, layout or an onboarding flow behind a flag Deleting or migrating customer data
A new library inside one service A public API contract other teams build on
An experiment shown to 5% of users Charges, refunds, anything that moves money
The order of the next three tickets Security and privacy promises to users
An internal tool or process tried for one sprint Hiring someone, or letting someone go

Treat the table as a rough guide. The same change can land in either column depending on how you ship it, which brings us to the next part.

Build the second direction on purpose

Plenty of choices feel final only because nobody has described the way back. You can often build one before you decide:

  • Put it behind a flag. Pete Hodgson's guide to feature toggles on Martin Fowler's site describes release toggles, which let unfinished code ship to production switched off, and ops toggles, which work as kill switches when something misbehaves (Feature Toggles).
  • Shrink the blast radius. Google's SRE workbook defines canarying as "a partial and time-limited deployment of a change in a service and its evaluation." A bad change reaches a small slice of production, and you can pause and roll back before everyone sees it (Canarying Releases).
  • Decide how you'll know. A rollback nobody knows when to trigger is a wish. Pick the metric or signal you'll watch before you ship.

On Zalo PC, we keep risky changes default off, behind a kill switch or remote config, so the way back is a config change instead of a late-night hotfix.

Flags have a price too. Hodgson points out that toggles add conditional logic and testing burden, and that "savvy teams view their Feature Toggles as inventory which comes with a carrying cost." He suggests release toggles shouldn't stick around much longer than a week or two. Building the way back includes a plan to remove it once the decision has settled.

Write the exit next to the decision

A habit worth stealing: write the reversal condition right where you record the decision. "If the error rate stays above 1% for an hour, roll back." "If support gets two tickets about this screen, rewrite the copy." "If adoption is flat after a week, remove the experiment." Those thresholds are examples, so pick ones that fit your product. Once the exit is visible, the decision stops feeling mysterious, and nobody has to relitigate it from memory a month later.

Some doors really are one-way

Reversibility doesn't excuse skipping the thinking. Money, trust, data, contracts and safety deserve slower movement and stronger review, and some changes can't be canaried or flagged at all. A migration that rewrites customer balances needs a different ceremony from a button label. Match the weight of the process to the real weight of the choice. If you can't tell yet which kind of door you're facing, waiting a bit for more context can be the right call (more on that in Wait for the Whole Story Before You Call It).

Reversible decisions are kinder to teams

When every decision feels permanent, people have to defend perfect foresight. They argue harder, hedge more and say less when they're unsure. When the way back is clear, people can say what they believe, name what they don't know, and agree on how the system will teach them the rest. The team stops carrying the whole future into one meeting. It carries a next step, a checkpoint and a way back, which is usually enough to move.

Try this week

  • In your next long decision meeting, ask: "What would it take to undo this in two weeks?"
  • Name the door: one-way or two-way? Size the process to match.
  • For a two-way door, write the rollback trigger next to the decision.
  • Put your next risky change behind a flag, and open a ticket to remove that flag later.

faqs.q: What's the difference between one-way and two-way door decisions?
faqs.a: Jeff Bezos used the terms in his 2015 shareholder letter. One-way doors are consequential and nearly irreversible, so they deserve slow, careful deliberation. Two-way doors can be changed or reversed, so they should be made quickly by a person with good judgment or a small group.

faqs.q: How do I make a decision easier to reverse?
faqs.a: Ship it behind a feature flag or kill switch, roll it out to a small slice of production first (a canary), and decide in advance which metric or signal will tell you to roll back. Write that rollback condition next to the decision.

faqs.q: Do feature flags have a downside?
faqs.a: Yes. Each toggle adds conditional logic and testing work. Pete Hodgson recommends treating toggles as inventory with a carrying cost, and suggests release toggles generally should not stay around much longer than a week or two.
